blocks.content: CAP Theorem Basics covered the tradeoff a database makes across multiple machines. OLTP versus OLAP closes out the Database Fundamentals module by looking at something different but equally foundational, the actual shape of the workload itself, since a database built for one kind of workload can genuinely struggle with the other.

OLTP and OLAP stand for online transaction processing and online analytical processing, and the distinction between them explains why many real companies run more than one kind of database system side by side, not out of redundancy, but because the two workloads genuinely pull in different directions.

1. How This Closes Out the Module
blocks.text: 1. How This Closes Out the Module

blocks.content: Looking back across the module makes the connection clear. Types of databases matched storage model to data shape. RDBMS versus NoSQL covered the schema and scale tradeoff. Database architecture covered the internal layers. ACID properties covered single machine guarantees. CAP theorem covered multi machine tradeoffs. OLTP versus OLAP closes the module by looking at the workload shape itself, a lens that cuts across every other topic already covered.
Every database choice covered earlier in this module ultimately gets applied to a real workload, and OLTP versus OLAP is the most fundamental split in what that workload actually looks like.

blocks.alt: How This Closes Out the Module

blocks.content: 2. The OLTP Shape

OLTP, online transaction processing, describes workloads made of many small, fast transactions, each one touching only a handful of rows at a time. Placing a single order, checking a single account balance, updating a single user profile, these are all genuinely OLTP operations.

An OLTP system is optimized for handling a huge volume of these small, fast operations reliably and quickly, often with many users hitting the system simultaneously, each one doing something small and specific.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438195272-271299126.png
{"headers":["Workload","Typical Query Shape"],"rows":[["OLTP","Small, fast, touching a handful of rows"],["OLAP","Large, complex, aggregating millions of rows"]]}
3. The OLAP Shape

OLAP, online analytical processing, describes workloads made of few, large, complex queries, each one reading and aggregating potentially millions of rows at once. Calculating total revenue by region across a full year is a genuinely OLAP operation, it touches an enormous number of individual order rows to produce one summary answer.

An OLAP system is optimized for handling these large, aggregate queries efficiently, even though there are far fewer of them running at any given moment compared to the constant stream of small OLTP transactions.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438195273-723380301.png
4. Why They Genuinely Conflict

Running heavy OLAP queries directly against your live OLTP database genuinely slows down the real, live transactions that database is also trying to serve, since a massive aggregate query consumes real resources, memory, disk access, processing time, that the small, fast transactions also need.

Separating OLTP and OLAP into different systems lets each workload stay fast without interfering with the other, the live transaction system stays responsive for real users, while the analytics system can run large, resource intensive queries without slowing anyone down.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438195273-558239871.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Running large analytical reports directly against a live, production OLTP database during peak hours. This genuinely risks slowing down real user facing transactions, exactly when the system needs to be at its most responsive.
5. A Worked Example
A concrete scenario shows this separation applied in practice. An e commerce platform genuinely benefits from running two distinct systems for these two distinct workloads.

The live orders database is genuinely OLTP, optimized for fast, individual transactions as customers actually place orders throughout the day. Data is then periodically copied out of that live system into a separate analytics warehouse, which is genuinely OLAP, optimized for large, aggregate queries like monthly revenue reports, without ever touching the live, production system directly.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438195273-110005518.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The periodic copy from an OLTP system into a separate OLAP warehouse is often called an ETL process, extract, transform, load, a pattern genuinely worth recognizing since it shows up constantly in real data engineering work.
6. Schema Design Genuinely Differs Too

An OLTP schema is typically normalized, minimizing duplication so that each individual small transaction stays fast and consistent, a topic covered in real depth in the later Normalization module of this course.

An OLAP schema is often deliberately denormalized instead, trading some duplication for genuinely faster aggregate queries, since joining fewer, wider tables is often faster for the kind of large scale aggregation OLAP workloads actually need.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438195273-222398837.png

8. A Quick Reference Query
A genuinely OLTP style query touches a small, specific set of rows, here checking one specific order.
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = 48213;
A genuinely OLAP style query aggregates across a huge number of rows to produce one summary answer, here total revenue by region for the past year.

SELECT region, SUM(order_total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY region;
